title: Quantum Measurement and Shots
summary: Understand the Born rule, why repeated shots are required, and how Qiskit orders the classical bits in a count string.
objectives: Use the Born rule to compute measurement probabilities.
Explain the difference between a quantum state and a classical result.
Read a two-qubit bitstring with c1 on the left and c0 on the right.
Interpret shots as repeated preparations and measurements.

sections.heading: One state, one classical record
body: Before measurement, the circuit evolves a quantum state. Measurement produces classical bits, and those bits are what the simulator returns.
The Born rule gives the probability of each outcome from the state's amplitudes. For a one-qubit state α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, the probability of observing 0 is |α|² and the probability of observing 1 is |β|².

sections.heading: Shots are repeated experiments
body: A single shot prepares the circuit, applies the gates, measures, and records one bitstring. Running 1,024 shots repeats this process 1,024 times.
The result is a histogram of classical outcomes. It is not a list of 1,024 different states, and it does not reveal the amplitudes directly. The counts estimate the measurement distribution.

callout.title: Observed versus theoretical
callout.text: An observed probability is count / shots. A theoretical probability comes from the state vector. With finite shots they need not match exactly, even when the simulator is ideal.

sections.heading: Bit order in Qiskit counts
body: Qiskit displays the highest-index classical bit on the left. For a two-qubit circuit with classical bits c0 and c1, a count string is written c1c0.
If you apply X to q1 and measure both qubits, the result is "10": c1 = 1 and c0 = 0. Reading the string left to right is not the same as reading qubit indices from low to high.
If a qubit is not measured, its classical bit remains 0 in the count string. That leading or trailing 0 is not evidence about the qubit's quantum state.

sections.heading: Compare three preparations
body: Measure |0⟩: every shot gives 0. Apply X and measure: every shot gives 1. Apply H and measure: shots split between 0 and 1.
The sample circuit is the deterministic X case, so it should return only "1". Switch to the superposition lesson to compare the statistical case.

expected_behavior: X followed by measurement returns "1" for every shot in the ideal simulator.
There is no spread because the state before measurement is a computational-basis state.
A two-qubit X on q1 would produce "10", because c1 is the leftmost character.

check_questions.question: For the state (|0⟩ + i|1⟩)/√2, what is P(1)?
check_questions.explanation: The amplitude of |1⟩ is i/√2. Its squared magnitude is |i|²/2 = 1/2, so P(1) = 0.5.

check_questions.question: A two-qubit circuit applies X to q1 and measures q0 and q1. Which count string should appear?
check_questions.explanation: Qiskit writes c1c0. q1 = 1 and q0 = 0, so the string is "10".

check_questions.question: Why does increasing shots not guarantee exactly 50/50 counts for H|0⟩?
options: Each shot is an independent sample, so finite samples fluctuate
The H gate is random in a way that changes the state
check_questions.explanation: The ideal probability is 1/2 for each outcome. A finite number of independent samples will usually deviate from the exact ratio.
